It's January 2032. The work on the ground-floor flat is behind schedule. Michael has found Susanne Lehmann: she's now called Susanne Albrecht and she's a teacher in Hanover. Ludwig wants to write two letters. Lena is helping him.
Lena, I have to write two letters and I haven't written a formal letter for twenty years. The first one is going to the building firm.
The Holzmann firm? They were supposed to be finished in December.
Exactly. The agreed date was the fifteenth of December. Now it's the middle of January, and the bathroom still has no tiles. The tradesmen only come twice a week.
Then we'll write a complaint. But politely. With anger you get nowhere with German firms. With deadlines you do.
What do I write as the subject?
“Complaint about the delay to the building works, Kastanienallee 31, ground floor.” Short and clear. Then: “Dear Sir or Madam”, because we don't have a name.
And then? What I'd like most is to write: you're a bunch of lazy donkeys.
Grandpa! No. You write: “I am contacting you because the agreed works have still not been completed.” Then the facts. And at the end: “I expect the works to be completed by the 15th of February.”
That sounds much more dangerous than lazy donkeys.
That's exactly the trick. And the second letter?
The second one is going to Susanne. To a woman I don't know, but whose secret sat in my wall for forty-two years. How do you begin a letter like that?
Formally. “Dear Mrs Albrecht.” She doesn't know you. But I think after the first sentence she'll suggest you use “du”.
“ich wende mich an Sie” = I am contacting you

It took Ludwig three evenings to write the letter to Susanne. He had written the letter to the building firm in an hour, with Lena's help, and he was proud of it: twelve factual sentences, two dates, a deadline, not a single swear word. But the letter to Susanne was something else. He wrote it by hand, with the old fountain pen Ingrid had given him for their twentieth wedding anniversary, on white paper. He tore up four drafts. He read the fifth to Lena at the kitchen table, one dark January evening, while Fritz snored under the table.

Before that he had told Lena about Ingrid's letters. In the GDR, he said, people didn't write complaints. They wrote “petitions”, to the housing office, to the district council, to the school authority. In forty years Ingrid had written over a hundred petitions: for a new roof for the school, for books that officially didn't exist, for a family whose children weren't being allowed into the upper secondary school. “She wrote very politely,” said Ludwig. “And very, very persistently. In the end she almost always won. The officials were afraid of her. Not because she was loud, but because she never gave up.”

Dear Mrs Albrecht, please forgive me for contacting you without having introduced myself. My name is Ludwig Brandt, I am eighty-three years old and since 1995 I have been the owner of the house at Kastanienallee 31 in Berlin. In November, during the renovation works on the ground floor, I found a tin box behind the tiled stove. I believe it belongs to you.

I have read your letter. I hope you will forgive me for that. You addressed it to whoever found the box, and that was me, so I took the liberty of opening it. You wrote: please be happy here. I would like to let you know that in February I will be moving into this flat. I promise you I will do my best.

I would be very grateful if you could let me know whether you would like the box back. I would gladly bring it to you in person. Yours sincerely, Ludwig Brandt. PS: Mirko lived in my flat. On the first floor. I have only just found out.

Lena was silent for a moment. Then she said: “The PS. That's the most important sentence in the whole letter.” Ludwig nodded. “I know. Ingrid always said that in a good letter the most important thing is either in the first sentence or in the PS. Never in the middle.” He folded the letter, put it in an envelope and wrote the address Michael had given him: Mrs Susanne Albrecht, Gymnasium am Lindenpark, Hanover. It had taken Michael four phone calls to find her.

The building firm's reply came four days later, by email, in perfect bureaucratic German: “Dear Mr Brandt, we regret the delay that has occurred, which is due to supply difficulties. We assure you that we will complete the works by the 10th of February. By way of compensation we will cover the cost of fitting an additional grab handle in the bathroom.” Ludwig read it three times and then laughed so loudly that Fritz woke up. “A grab handle! For lazy donkeys they wouldn't have given me anything.”

Susanne's reply came ten days later. Ludwig had looked in the letterbox every day, twice, morning and afternoon, and each time had pretended he didn't care. Then, one grey Thursday, it was there: a thick envelope, with round, neat handwriting that Ludwig recognised immediately. It was the handwriting from the blue school exercise book. Only it had grown up.

Dear Mr Brandt, I opened your letter during the long break, in the staff room, and my colleagues had never seen me cry. Now they have. I haven't forgotten the box for forty-two years. Every time I was in Berlin, I walked along Kastanienallee and didn't dare to ring the bell. I was afraid someone had ripped out the stove. That everything had gone.

And one more thing: your name. Brandt. When I read it, I had to sit down. My first teacher was called Brandt. Mrs Ingrid Brandt, at the primary school on Kastanienallee, from 1981 to 1985. She taught me to read, at our home, on the ground floor, every Wednesday afternoon, because at school I was too slow and my mother was ashamed. She never took any money for it. Is it possible that you… that she… I am enclosing a photograph. Please tell me if I am mistaken.

I became a German teacher, as I wrote back then. For thirty years I have been teaching children to read and write. Please keep the box. It belongs to the house, not to me. But I would like to see it once. And the flat. If you will allow me, I will come when you move in, in February.

PS: Mirko. I never saw him again. We wrote letters to each other for two years, then it ended, the way things end when you're sixteen. I don't know what became of him. Sometimes I think it's the only thing in my life I would like to know.

In the envelope was a small black-and-white photograph with a scalloped edge. A class, twenty-five children in two rows in front of a blackboard, 1981, Year 1. In the second row, a little girl with plaits looking seriously at the camera. And next to the class, with a book under her arm and the laugh Ludwig had seen every morning for almost fifty years, stood a young teacher. Ludwig didn't need to look for long. He took off his glasses, didn't wipe them, put them back on and looked once more, just to be sure he wasn't dreaming. Then he took the old album out of the cupboard in the hall, leafed through to 1981 and found the same photograph, stuck in, with Ingrid's handwriting underneath: “Class 1b, 1981. The little one with the plaits reads the worst and wants it the most. She'll make something of herself.”

Lena dropped by that evening with a slice of apple cake and found her grandfather at the kitchen table, with two identical photographs in front of him, an old album and a letter, and with an expression she couldn't read. “Grandpa? Has something happened?” Ludwig pushed the two photographs towards her without a word. Lena looked at them, read Ingrid's sentence under the stuck-in picture, then Susanne's letter, and slowly sat down. “Grandma knew her,” she whispered. “Grandma taught her to read. And then she became a teacher. Because of Grandma.” Ludwig nodded. “She never told me. She never said anything about it. Hundreds of children, Lena. How many Susannes are out there that we know nothing about?”

Ludwig put the letter on the table and looked out of the window for a long time, at the bare chestnut trees. Then he picked up the phone and called Michael. “She's replied,” he said. “She's coming in February. And Michael: you know all the school authorities. Do you also know someone who knows musicians?” Michael laughed at the other end. “Mr Brandt, you're not thinking of…” “Oh yes,” said Ludwig. “That's exactly what I'm thinking. Mirko Petrović. He wanted to be a musician. He played the guitar badly. That's all we know. But we didn't know much more about Susanne either.”

That night Ludwig wrote another letter, the third in a month, this time without Lena's help. It was short and informal, to a woman who after a single letter had given him the feeling that he had known her for years. “Dear Susanne,” he wrote, “if I may. No, you're not mistaken. Ingrid was my wife, for forty-seven years. Please come. The flat is waiting. And the tiled stove. And bring an appetite, my granddaughter bakes the best apple cake in Prenzlauer Berg. With love, your Ludwig.” He read it twice. Then he crossed out “Sie” and wrote above it, in small letters: “du”. Ingrid, he thought, would have liked that.
